title: Foreign Investors Just Poured a Record $4.2 Billion into Indian Government Bonds — and a Bigger Prize May Be Coming
excerpt: India's bond market is attracting its largest-ever monthly foreign inflow after tax exemptions and expanded access. The real catalyst: potential inclusion in Bloomberg's flagship global bond index, which could unlock $20-30 billion more.
body:
Something unusual is happening in India's bond market. Even as foreign portfolio investors continue to sell Indian equities at a furious pace — pulling out ₹2.87 lakh crore ($34 billion) so far in 2026 — a record wave of foreign money is flowing into the other side of the ledger: Indian government bonds.

In June alone, FPIs have purchased ₹39,640 crore (approximately $4.2 billion) worth of Indian government securities, smashing the previous monthly record of ₹22,005 crore set in August 2024. The surge nearly doubled the prior high in a single month, and the pace has accelerated since the government and Reserve Bank of India unveiled a sweeping set of reforms on June 5.

The contrast is stark. In the equity market, 2026 has been defined by relentless foreign selling — the worst year for FPI outflows on record. But in the bond market, the same class of investors is arriving in unprecedented numbers. The divergence tells a story about what India did right in an otherwise difficult year.

## What Changed on June 5

The catalyst was a coordinated package of policy measures designed to attract foreign capital into India's sovereign debt market:

The government scrapped both capital gains tax and withholding tax on foreign investments in government bonds — effectively making returns tax-free for overseas investors.

The RBI expanded the Fully Accessible Route (FAR), the pool of government securities that foreigners can purchase without any investment caps, to include bonds with maturities of up to 30 years. Previously, the eligible pool was narrower and shorter-dated.

Additional measures to support the rupee — including subsidized hedging costs on foreign-currency deposits and incentives for overseas borrowing by Indian companies — were announced simultaneously.



> **"In June alone, FPIs have purchased ₹39,640 crore (approximately $4.2 billion) worth of Indian government securities, smashing the previous monthly record of ₹22,005 crore set in August 2024."**


The result was immediate. In the first two weeks after the announcement, more than $2 billion of FAR bonds were purchased by foreign investors — matching the total inflow from the previous eight months combined.

"We believe that these changes are a game-changer for debt flows," said Jennifer Taylor, head of emerging market debt at State Street Investment Management, which manages about $5.6 trillion in assets.

## The Bloomberg Index Prize

The tax exemptions were not just about attracting capital in the short term. They were designed with a specific strategic target: India's inclusion in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Bond Index, the flagship benchmark tracked by trillions of dollars in global fixed-income portfolios.

India was added to JPMorgan's emerging market bond index in 2024, triggering roughly $10 billion in passive inflows. But the Bloomberg index is substantially larger. Economists estimate that inclusion could unlock $20 to $30 billion in passive foreign investment over the 10 months following inclusion, as global bond funds mechanically adjust their portfolios to match the index's new weights.

Bloomberg Index Services is expected to seek investor feedback this month on whether Indian government bonds should be added. Multiple global asset managers have signalled support.

"RBI's measures have alleviated concerns regarding rupee depreciation, while tax exemptions for FPIs have boosted optimism about India's potential inclusion in Bloomberg's global aggregate index," said Sameer Karyatt, managing director and head of trading at DBS Bank. "These factors have prompted some investors to invest proactively in India."

Niel Clement, portfolio manager for emerging market fixed income at BNP Paribas Asset Management (which manages more than €1.6 trillion), said the reforms would "broaden opportunities for overseas investors, redirect flows to the onshore market, and provide a constructive boost to India's bid for inclusion."

## Market Effects Already Visible

The inflows have had a tangible stabilising effect. The rupee, which had hit a record low of 96.96 per dollar in late May, recovered to close at 94.40 by late June — a significant rebound. The 10-year benchmark bond yield has eased by 20 basis points since the policy measures were announced, closing at 6.76 per cent. Foreign exchange reserves stood at $672 billion as of June 12.

Citi sharply revised India's balance of payments forecast for the current fiscal year, now expecting a $5 billion surplus versus an earlier projected deficit of $60 billion — a swing of $65 billion driven primarily by the policy package.

## Risks and Caveats

Not everyone is fully convinced. The June surge stands in stark contrast to the broader fiscal-year picture: net FPI inflows into FAR bonds for the full year stood at just ₹3,546 crore before the June sprint. Some analysts caution against reading too much into a single month.

"The bigger issue for offshore investors is still the currency," said Rong Ren Goh, head of macro and thematics for Asian fixed income at Eastspring Investments. "Investors are likely to wait for clearer signs of rupee stability before raising allocations." The rupee remains down nearly 6 per cent for the year and elevated US Treasury yields continue to limit the relative appeal of Indian debt.

M&G Investments' Low Guan Yi struck a more measured note: "The broader investment backdrop for bonds remains challenging, given the pickup in interest-rate volatility across many markets and the shift from monetary easing to tightening in response to inflationary pressures from energy and food prices."

## What NRI Investors Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora, the bond reforms are part of a broader pattern of measures designed to attract overseas capital back to India. Combined with the recently announced subsidized FCNR-B deposit scheme — which allows NRIs to earn 6-7 per cent on dollar deposits without currency risk — the government is building an increasingly attractive toolkit for diaspora investors.

The key question now is whether Bloomberg will include Indian bonds in its flagship index. If it does, the $4.2 billion that arrived in June will look like a warm-up act. If it does not, the sustainability of the inflows will depend on how long the tax incentives and rupee stability hold. Either way, for the first time in 2026, India's fixed-income market is drawing global capital rather than repelling it — and that shift is worth watching closely.
